To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

whole‐body irradiated mice show an increase in the number of natural killer (NK), T lymphocyte and monocyte/macrophage cells in the spleen, and that this increase in NK cell numbers is associated with an increase in natural suppressive activity.

whole‐body irradiaton causes differential radiosensitivity in the major mononuclear cell population in the mouse splean, and that the balance of recovery‐enhancing and recovery‐inhibitory cells following irradiation may provide an indication (biological dosimeter) of the degree of damage.
ionizing radiation causes decreased spleen cell numbers and decreased ability of remaining SMNC to respond in mitogen‐stimulated proliferation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the characterization of SMNC populations following whole‐body radiation exposure and the development of FCA protocols to determine the role of these populations in radiation‐induced immune suppression and haematopoietical recovery.

the identification, characterization, and quantification of the various SMNC populations in the irradiated mouse spleen, and the determination of their relative radiosensitivity, as well as their potential roles in immune suppression and haematopoietics.
the characterization of splenic cell populations in the mouse, and the effects of whole‐body irradiaton on these cell populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
radiation causes a selective decrease in the number of splenic T cells, B cells, monocytes/macrophage, and an increase in NK cells and activated MNC.
ionizing radiation causes differential damage to splenic mononucleated cells.

the spleen is the most radiosensitive organ in the body and that the spleen contains all of the cell populations necessary to cause the immunological and haematological changes seen after radiation exposure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relative composition of MNC in the mouse spleens changes after irradiation.

radiation‐induced changes in splenic monocyte/macrophages, B lymphocytes, CD4+ and CD45+ T cells and NK cells, may contribute to the immunosuppressive effects of radiation and may be involved in the recovery of haematopoiesis.
the spleen contains a heterogeneous mixture of cells with differential radiosensitivities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the balance of recovery‐enhancing T lymphocytes and recovery‐inhibitory NK cells following irradiation may influence the extent of haematopoiesis.

ionizing radiation causes differential alterations in splenic monocyte/macrophage (M/M) populations and that these changes may play a role both in active immune suppression (e.g. natural suppressor cells) as well as in the recovery of haematopoiesis following radiation exposure.
radiation‐induced alterations in the relative proportion of splenic MNC populations can provide a useful indication of the extent and nature of the damage.
